15319-the-government-class-book-designed:
Andrew Young's Government Class Book, entered in 1859 and printed in New York in 1865, teaches youth the principles of constitutional government and the rights and duties of citizens. Questions once printed at the foot of each page now appear collected at the end. Young also wrote on civil government and law.

The preface argues that a self-governing people must spread political knowledge, since American government is complex and needs informed citizens. Lessons walk through constitutions, offices, and duties in clear order. Students of civic education will find the book a plain, earnest sample of its kind.
24475-the-nursery-february-1873-vol-xiii:
Issued at Boston in February 1873, this was the second number of volume thirteen of The Nursery, a monthly magazine for youngest readers. Its prose opens with the biography of a bubble, told by a papa, and goes on to a little duck, a Thanksgiving dinner, a grandpa story, and a new dog.

Other pieces tell of Bunny, Dandy the bear, and a dog and his shadow, with Little Mischief as a regular feature. Verses include Jack's Menagerie, Jack Frost, Sue's Seasons, and The Children's Party, with Jack and Jill set to music. The issue mixes humour and kindness in short pieces a small child could enjoy.
26280-the-renewal-of-life-how-and-when-t:
Margaret Warner Morley's 1906 book, issued by A. C. McClurg in Chicago, guides parents on how and when to tell children the facts of life. Its opening states the puzzle plainly: every child must learn where life comes from, yet parents long for a high ideal to guard the telling. Morley argues for truth told in good time, through nature rather than through shame or silence.

Chapters move from seed growth and flower fertilization to lessons from fish, amphibians, birds, and mammals. Pollen grains, ovaries, and protoplasm, the living stuff of plants and animals, get clear, simple explanations. A closing list of helpful books aids further study. The book offers a gentle, science-based path for a delicate talk.
28134-the-nursery-june-1877-vol-xxi-no-6:
The Nursery for June 1877, volume twenty-one, number six, closes the volume with summer tales for youngest readers. Arthur's New Sloop leads the prose, as Uncle Martin teaches boys to handle a model boat in a squall, with lessons on sail, rudder, and steering for the open sea. Other tales cover a true story, playing soldier, a visit to grandma, and a fisherman's return.

Verse includes Tot's Turnover, the kingfisher, Bye-Lo-Land, and June, with a fifth astronomy lesson and notes on crickets. The issue, published in Boston by John L. Shorey, suits children learning to read through boats, pets, and country days.
31951-geographic-distribution-and-taxono:
John A. White's 1953 paper for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History studies the geographic distribution and taxonomy of the chipmunks of Wyoming. Its contents move from purpose, methods, and materials through variation in juveniles, young, subadults, adults, and old adults, to a key to the species inhabiting Wyoming.

Accounts of species and subspecies follow, including Eutamias minimus and its forms, Eutamias amoenus, Eutamias dorsalis, and Eutamias umbrinus, with review and conclusions. Readers get a concise faunal taxonomy, mapping where Wyoming's chipmunks live and how their local forms differ.
32733-the-journal-of-lieut-john-l-harden:
Lieutenant John L. Hardenbergh of the Second New York Continental Regiment kept this journal from May 1 to October 3, 1779, during General Sullivan's campaign against the western Indians. It appeared as number one of the Cayuga County Historical Society collections, printed at Auburn in 1879 in two hundred and fifty copies.

Hardenbergh, born at Rosendale in Ulster County in 1748, was the youngest of seven children of Leonard and Rachel Hardenbergh. His journal is joined by parts of the journals of Major Beatty, Thomas Grant, George Grant, and Colonel Dearborn. Together they record Clinton's march, the battle of Newtown, the Groveland ambuscade, and the Indian towns destroyed.
35809-rulers-of-india-the-earl-of-mayo:
Earl of Mayo is a volume in the Rulers of India series, edited by Sir William Wilson Hunter. Hunter wrote this life himself. The Oxford edition was printed in eighteen ninety one, with a map of the Indian empire. A portrait of Mayo serves as frontispiece. Spelling of names follows the system of the Imperial Gazetteer, a note says.

Contents run to nine chapters and an index. After an introduction, a long chapter treats the man himself. The actual process of viceregal government comes next. Dealings with the feudatory states and foreign policy follow. Finance reforms, military policy, and internal administration take their own chapters. A final chapter is called The End. Mayo was born in Dublin in eighteen twenty two, the text says.
38826-bolanyo:
Opie Read wrote Bolanyo, a novel put out by Way and Williams at Chicago in 1897. Maxfield Parrish made the cover, and Charles Francis Browne made the decorations. The book opens on the river, in the air, and with a black giant. Later chapters bring a senator, a state treasurer, and a man called Bugg Peters. A moment of forgiveness, a visit to Mrs. Estell, and the charm of an old town fill the middle of the book.

Old Joe Vark and old Aunt Patsey add local color, and a play, a slow step on the stairs, and a dark alley add suspense. A ringing bell and magnolia land point to Southern scenes. The tale closes with scoundrel craft brought to light. Readers get a brisk, folksy tale of river folk and small-town wiles.
39163-the-war-tiger-or-adventures-and-wo:
The War Tiger, or Adventures and Wonderful Fortunes of the Young Sea Chief and his Lad Chow, is William Dalton's tale of the conquest of China. J B Lippincott and Company of Philadelphia published it in 1884, with illustrations by H S Melville. Dalton had written The White Elephant.

His preface sketches the fall of the Ming for young readers. The last Ming emperor sank from wisdom into pleasure, magistrates oppressed the people, famine bred rebellion, and petty kings carved up the provinces. The Mantchou Tartars rode on the capital province while generals like Woo-san-Kwei held them off and others turned their arms on the throne. Out of the anarchy rose Chin-Chi-Loong, a pirate to his enemies and a patriot to his friends, the sea chief of the story's world. Against that China, Dalton sets his young hero and the lad Chow.
40753-the-nursery-february-1881-vol-xxix:
The Nursery for February 1881, volume twenty nine, number two, is a monthly magazine for the youngest readers, published at Boston. The number mixes short prose pieces with verse, all pitched to small children. Pictures go with many of the pieces.

The lead prose piece, Almost Ready for Launching, shows a ship on the stocks with twenty six men at work. It explains the trade of the calkers, who drive oakum into the seams between planks and cover it with hot pitch. Other pieces tell of a boy's new plant, a kite that would not fly, and Bertie at his uncle's. Verse includes The Would-be Travellers, A Queer Kitten, and The Snow-Fairies. A nursery song with music closes the number.
42158-the-nursery-september-1881-vol-xxx:
The Nursery for September 1881 is one issue of a monthly magazine made for the youngest readers. It was printed in Boston by the Nursery Publishing Company. The volume is number thirty, and the issue is number three. Its pages mix short prose tales with verse, songs, and pictures meant for small children.

The prose list holds tales such as Home in Sight, Nellie and Kitty, The Prisoner, and The Pet Fawn. The verse list holds Contentment, The Brook, Blueberrying, and The Morning Sail, which comes with music. Home in Sight opens with a sea captain calling tired passengers on deck to see land near Cape Cod. The issue shows how early reading for young children paired gentle stories with poems and song.
51180-santa-claus-gets-his-wish-a-christ:
Santa Claus Gets His Wish is a Christmas play in one act, sold in the Baker’s Edition of Plays at Boston for twenty five cents. The Walter Baker Company issued the piece for amateur use. Its list of plays for colleges and high schools fills the front pages. Each play in that list is marked with its cast size, time, price, and royalty.

Such catalogues show how amateur drama worked in that age. A school or a club could pick a play by the number of men and women it needed. Times run from half an hour to near three hours in the list. The Santa Claus play itself was made for young performers at the holiday season. One act and a small price kept it within reach of any school hall. The book is a sample of the trade in ready made plays.
51896-popular-pastimes-for-field-and-fir:
Popular Pastimes for Field and Fireside, or Amusements for Young and Old, was carefully compiled by Aunt Carrie and published by Milton Bradley and Company at Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1867. Aunt Carrie dedicates the book to her young friends, hoping it will add to their home pleasures.

Her preface argues home influence before any list of games. Parents, she says, must sympathize with their children and never forget they were children themselves; an hour a day spent playing with them beats every moment spent earning money for them. The pleasantest hour is twilight, when the family gathers and children should be drawn out to confide in their parents.
52371-armenia-and-the-armenians-a-list-o:
Ida Pratt compiled this list of references on Armenia and the Armenians. The New York Public Library printed it in the year 1919. Richard Gottheil directed the work as its Oriental Division chief. The list holds works held March 1, 1919, in reference rooms.

Contents run bibliography, periodicals, geography, and old remains first. History takes a long section, with massacres at pages past thirty. Church, missions, the Armenian question, and folk lore follow in order. Gottheil prefatory note calls the Armenians a remarkable, pitiable race. Language, inscriptions, and literature of Armenia take long list sections of their own.
59041-sermons-preached-at-the-church-of-:
Sermons preached at the Church of St Paul the Apostle in New York during the year 1861 fill this volume, printed in New York that same year. The preface says that friends who heard the sermons asked to see them in print. It also points to a wider want: Catholic sermons in English were scarce, which alone might justify the book.

No showy writing is promised. The preface states that the sermons make no pretence to brilliant passages, flowers of style, or appeals to popular feeling. Instead, the writers trust they will be found plain, simple, and direct. Their hope is that Catholic readers gain a clearer view of doctrine or duty, and a thought to lift the heart to God.
63527-cosmic-yo-yo:
Cosmic Yo-Yo is a science fiction tale by Ross Rocklynne, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1945. A mock notice at the head offers asteroids delivered cheap to your backyard, trouble handled without charge, by the Interplanetary Hauling Company. The tale that follows takes that joke and runs with it across the Belt.

Bob Parker stares through the photo-amplifiers at a wedge shaped asteroid and can hardly believe his luck. He and Queazy, whose full name is Quentin Zuyler, check its shape against an ethergram and find it matches to the last measure. A fortune in reward hangs on what the rock is made of, and they clamp their ship to its smooth face to test it.
65870-home-life-in-tokyo:
Home Life in Tokyo is a descriptive book by Jukichi Inouye, issued at Tokyo in 1910 with many illustrations. In his preface Inouye states his aim in plain terms. He means to give a concise account of the life his people lead at home in Tokyo. Many fine books on Japan exist, he grants, but most are by Europeans or Americans.

Those writers look at Japanese life from a western point of view, he says. A description by a native of the country might still hold interest, he thought. Works in English by his countrymen treat grave subjects, he notes. They do not touch such homely matters as he deals with here. That gap is the book's reason for being, and its pictures of autumn herbs show its eye for daily detail.
britannica-1911-bulawayo:
Bulawayo is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was the capital of Matabeleland, the western province of southern Rhodesia in South Africa. The entry gives its white population in nineteen hundred four. Set on high land between the Limpopo and Zambezi rivers, it lay far north east of Cape Town by rail.

Inside, readers find a town laid out in a clear grid around a large market square. Roads run in straight lines, with avenues east and west and streets north and south. Rhodes Street runs through the centre of the square. Rail lines link the town to the coast and north toward the Victoria Falls.
britannica-1911-cetywayo:
Cetywayo was king of the Zulus, eldest son of a king and nephew of two kings before him. He was a young man when his father was set on the throne with the aid of Dutch settlers of Natal. Three years on, Natal became a British colony, and the map of his world changed round him.

He had much of the war gift of his famed uncle, who built the Zulu war system, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He chafed at his fathers peace line toward British and Dutch neighbors. In doubt that his father favored a younger son as heir, he made war on that brother and slew him in a great fight by a river. The next year the nation set the old king aside in fact, and gave rule to Cetywayo, though the title stayed with his father.
britannica-1911-enomoto-buyo:
Buyo Enomoto, a Japanese naval officer who lived from 1839 to 1909, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Tokyo and was the first officer sent by the Tokugawa state to learn sea craft in Europe. He trained in Holland and sailed home in charge of a frigate built at Amsterdam. His name rests on one wild act.

In charge of most of Japan's sea force, he would not yield when the Shogun fell. He steamed north and set up a republic at Hakodate, but soon had to give in. The new state jailed him in place of the death such a deed once earned. Four years on, it gave him a high post in the same north land. He later held the seals for posts, schools, and foreign affairs, and rose to viscount in 1885.
britannica-1911-thayetmyo:
Thayetmyo, a town and district of Upper Burma, is given a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town stands on the right bank of the Irrawaddy, across from Allanmyo. Its count in 1901 was 15,824, and it holds a British battalion wing and a native regiment. The town is famed for good health and for silver work.

The district spans 4,750 square miles and held 239,706 people in 1901, down four per cent in ten years. Ranges hem it east and west, and much of the land is wooded hills. The Irrawaddy runs its length from north to south. Salt and hot springs occur, oil is found, and lime quarries work near the town. Chief crops are rice, cotton, oil seeds, and tobacco. Wild life runs from elephants and tigers to silver pheasants. The district was made in 1870 and moved to Upper Burma in 1896.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bagamoyo:
Bagamoyo was a vicariate apostolic in German East Africa, cut off on 11 May 1906 from Northern Zanzibar. Its Catholics numbered 14,728, in a colony of about 6,700,000 natives, mostly of Bantu tribes. The Holy Ghost Fathers, fifty-two strong, and eight Trappists staffed the mission, aided by two women's congregations. Its first vicar apostolic, Franz Xaver Vogt, was elected on 25 July 1906.

The vicariate held fifteen churches and chapels, fifteen stations with medical service, and fifteen orphanages. It ran six trade and farm schools, seventy-one schools with 7,574 native pupils, two leper stations, and two hospitals. The vicar lived at Bagamoyo, a small seaport near the Kingani mouth, opposite Zanzibar island. That town formed the center of the colony's telegraph and cable systems.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcelino-men:
Marcelino Menendez y Pelayo was a Spanish poet, historian, and literary critic, born at Santander in 1856 and dead there in 1912. He studied first at home, then at Barcelona from 1871, winning teachers' and government's admiration and funds for research. At twenty-two he took the Madrid chair of literature, and three years later joined the Spanish Academy.

His Heterodoxos Espanoles of 1880 traces Spain's political and literary story against the Catholic Church from Priscilian to his own day. Los origenes de la novela en Espana treated the Spanish novel's birth, while Ciencia espanola of 1887 argued Spain rich in philosophy and science and claimed the Inquisition fostered, not hindered, culture. He led the Royal Academy of History, edited Lope de Vega and lyric anthologies, and was judged the finest Spanish stylist since the Golden Age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-may:
Mayo, Irish Magh Eo, Plain of the Oaks or, by another account, Plain of the Yews, stood in modern Mayo parish between Claremorris and Castlebar. Its founder Colman, flourishing about the mid-seventh century, likely came from western Ireland and studied at Iona under Abbot Segenius. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a bishop who lost the Easter argument and left.

After Finian, second bishop of Lindisfarne, died, Colman succeeded him. His episcopate was troubled by a fierce renewal of the Easter controversy. Colman urged the old Irish custom, citing his predecessors, but at Whitby in 664 the Roman way of reckoning Easter won. Unwilling to drop the practice of Ireland's holy elders, Colman quit Lindisfarne for good and in 668 sailed home to found Mayo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colman-of-:
St. Colman of Mayo was founder of the Abbey and Diocese of Mayo, born in Connacht about 605. He died 8 August 676. This entry follows a man who took Iona's monastic habit; his virtues and learning grew so famous — St. Bede testifies to them — that on St. Finan's death in 661 he was appointed Bishop of Lindisfarne. The Synod of Whitby met in 664 during his brief episcopacy.

At that synod, Colman being a determined protagonist of the old Irish computation, the decision of King Oswy on the Paschal controversy led him to resign his see. Between 665 and 667 he set up several churches in Scotland, then sailed for Ireland with thirty disciples, settling at Innisboffin, County Mayo, in 668. Within three years he had built an abbey for Mayo's English monks alone, later called Mayo of the Saxons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tokio-tokyo:
Tokyo is an archdiocese covering twenty-one provinces of Japan, with over sixteen million people in its bounds. From 1866 to 1876 Japan formed a single vicariate under Petitjean, its first vicar apostolic. In 1876 it split into north and south, with Osouf ruling the north from Tokyo. In 1891 Leo XIII set up the Japanese hierarchy, making Osouf Archbishop of Tokyo with Nagasaki, Osaka and Hakodate as suffragans.

When Petitjean first visited the region in 1866 he found only two missionaries at Yokohama and a few dozen Japanese converts. Growth came under Osouf's thirty years, during which he built Tokyo cathedral in 1878 and became the pope's first envoy to the emperor. By 1911 the archdiocese counted an archbishop, twenty-seven missionaries, two native priests, twenty-three catechists and 9,858 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-virgin-of-cuy:
The Virgin of Cuyo, Our Lady of Cuyo or Our Lady of Carmel of Mendoza. Is a statue venerated in Mendoza, Argentina, from the earliest Spanish settlers, its origin uncertain but its antiquity undoubted. According to one historian it is probably the statue given with its church to the Franciscans when the Jesuits were expelled in 1767.

After an earthquake ruined that church in 1864 the Franciscans built the new church where it is now honoured. Its fame owes more to national gratitude than to its countless reported miracles. After fighting Napoleon in Spain he returned at independence's outbreak, gathered a small army in Cuyo, the territory now San Luis, San Juan. Mendoza, and led it to repeated success before setbacks against Peru's viceroy.
doe-osti-3030809-accelerating-hydrogen-r:
Andrew Whittaker of the University at Buffalo led this equipment project under award DE-EE0010674, running from February 2024 to January 2026. It was a congressionally directed buy meant to speed hydrogen research in New York. The gear went into two Buffalo departments: Chemical and Biological Engineering, and Materials Design and Innovation. Hydrogen is eyed as a synthetic fuel for clean energy and clean industry, and the labs needed tools to match that push.

The budget was 250,000 dollars, split as two purchases of 125,000 dollars each, one per department. The technical team joined three senior professors: Whittaker, a civil engineer, Mark Swihart, a chemical engineer, and Krishna Rajan, a materials scientist. The report covers what was bought, where it was installed, and the research it now supports.
podcast-joerogan-GIvY_pYcMYo:
New video of a UFO over a California military base gets reviewed in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rogan watches the footage and works through what it seems to show: lights, movement, and the reactions of the people who filmed it.

He compares the clip with earlier military sightings and asks what would make this one stronger or weaker as evidence. The talk touches on hoaxes, sensor tricks, and why bases draw so many reports. The segment is a small case study in how the show handles fresh UFO material: curious first, cautious second, and honest that a video alone settles little.
the-government-class-book-designed-for-t:
Andrew W. Young wrote The Government Class Book. It was designed for the instruction of youth. It teaches the principles of constitutional government and the rights and duties of citizens. It was printed in New York in 1865. It was entered for copyright in 1859. Young also wrote a Science of Government and First Lessons in Civil Government.

His preface argues a clear point. A people who govern themselves need political knowledge spread wide. The United States form of government is highly complex. It is well fit to promote the general welfare. But the knowledge to run it well takes much study. A large share of Americans lack that knowledge. Young says it will never become general until it is taught in schools. The class book is his means to that end. It makes civics a school subject for young citizens.
